cards.back: **Ecological tolerance** is the range of values of an environmental factor, such as temperature, within which a species can survive. Tolerance is measured one factor at a time.
cards.hint: Think about a trout and the cold water it needs.

cards.front: Along a gradient such as temperature, where does a species perform best?
cards.back: It performs best in the **optimum range**, near the middle of the gradient, where it grows and reproduces most. Performance drops toward both ends, first into zones of stress and then beyond the limits of tolerance.

cards.front: Why can a species be excluded from a place even when most conditions there suit it?
cards.back: One condition that lies outside the species' tolerance limits is a **limiting factor**. It prevents survival there, even if every other condition is suitable.

cards.front: What is a zone of stress?
cards.back: The **zone of stress** is the part of a tolerance gradient outside the optimum. Organisms can survive there, but their growth and reproduction decline.
cards.hint: Compare it with the optimum range and the limits of tolerance.

cards.front: What mistake is made when a species in its zone of stress is treated as dead?
cards.back: **Mistake:** assuming it cannot survive. Individuals in a zone of stress are still alive, but they grow and reproduce less.

cards.front: What is an adaptation in this topic?
cards.back: An **adaptation** is an inherited trait that increases survival or reproductive success in a particular environment. It spreads through a population over many generations.
cards.hint: Think about how traits pass from parents to offspring.

cards.front: How do behavior and body processes differ from adaptation as responses to changing conditions?
cards.back: Behavior and body processes help one individual within its lifetime, while **adaptation** changes a whole population over many generations. No response can take an organism beyond its limits of tolerance.
cards.hint: Consider how long each kind of response takes to work.

cards.back: A **generalist species** has broad tolerance limits and varied resource use, so it can live in many environments.
A **specialist species** has narrow tolerance limits or specific resource needs, so it can live in only a few environments. The giant panda is one example.

cards.front: Why are specialist species more vulnerable when conditions change?
cards.back: They have narrow tolerance limits and little room to adjust, so a small shift can push a factor past their limits. Generalists can cope with a wider range of conditions.
cards.hint: Think about how much change a narrow range can absorb.

cards.front: A fish has limits of $6$ and $28\,^\circ\text{C}$, optimum $14$ to $22\,^\circ\text{C}$. How is it affected at $10\,^\circ\text{C}$?
cards.back: It is in a **zone of stress**. $10\,^\circ\text{C}$ is above its lower limit of $6\,^\circ\text{C}$ but below the optimum, so it survives with reduced growth and reproduction.
cards.hint: Locate 10 °C relative to the limits and the optimum first.

cards.front: How does the same fish fare at $31\,^\circ\text{C}$?
cards.back: It **cannot survive**. $31\,^\circ\text{C}$ is above its upper limit of $28\,^\circ\text{C}$, so it lies beyond its limits of tolerance.

cards.front: Why might warming force a species to move toward the poles or higher up slopes?
cards.back: Warming can push places near a species' warm edge beyond its **upper temperature limit**. It then survives only where conditions still fall within its limits, and species that cannot move may disappear locally.
cards.hint: Think about where the warm edge of its range sits.
